column1: A kilometer contains 1000 meters.|T|The prefix kilo means a factor of one thousand.
A square kilometer contains 1000 square meters.|F|Square the length conversion: one square kilometer contains one million square meters.
Density is mass divided by volume.|T|Its SI unit is kilograms per cubic meter.
A measurement can be precise but inaccurate.|T|Repeated values can cluster closely while all being displaced from the true value.
Adding a length directly to a time produces a physically meaningful length.|F|Terms added in a physical equation must have compatible dimensions.
The SI base unit of time is the second.|T|Minutes and hours are useful units, but the second is the SI base unit.
Changing units changes the physical size of the measured object.|F|The number changes to compensate for the unit size; the object itself does not change.
Dimensional consistency alone proves an equation is physically correct.|F|It cannot detect an incorrect dimensionless coefficient or every incorrect physical relationship.
An order-of-magnitude estimate emphasizes an approximate scale rather than exact digits.|T|It identifies the nearest useful power-of-ten scale based on reasonable assumptions.
Displacement can be zero even when distance traveled is positive.|T|A round trip returns to the start but still covers a nonzero path length.
A negative velocity means an object is slowing down.|F|It means motion in the chosen negative direction; slowing depends on acceleration relative to velocity.
The slope of a position-time graph is velocity.|T|Slope gives position change per unit time.
The slope of a velocity-time graph is acceleration.|T|Acceleration measures how quickly velocity changes.
Signed area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement.|T|Negative velocity contributes negative displacement.
Constant acceleration requires constant velocity.|F|Nonzero constant acceleration produces a steadily changing velocity.
At the highest point of a vertical toss, gravitational acceleration is zero.|F|Velocity is momentarily zero, but gravity continues to accelerate the object downward.
A body speeds up when velocity and acceleration point in the same direction.|T|Acceleration then increases the magnitude of the velocity.
The constant-acceleration formulas may be used without checking whether acceleration is constant.|F|Their derivation assumes constant acceleration over the interval being analyzed.
A vector can be translated without changing its components if its magnitude and direction stay fixed.|T|A free vector represents directed magnitude rather than a unique starting location.
Vector addition depends on the order of the vectors.|F|Vector addition is commutative; the sum is the same in either order.
The magnitude of a vector must equal the sum of its components.|F|Perpendicular components combine by the Pythagorean relation, not simple addition.
Multiplying a nonzero vector by a negative scalar reverses its direction.|T|The magnitude is multiplied by the scalar’s absolute value.
The dot product of perpendicular vectors is zero.|T|Their angle has zero cosine.
The cross product is commutative.|F|Reversing the order negates the cross product.
A unit vector specifies direction with magnitude one.|T|It can multiply a scalar magnitude to represent a vector in that direction.
Two vectors with equal magnitudes must be equal.|F|They must also have the same direction to be equal.
A vector’s components depend on the coordinate axes used.|T|Rotating the axes changes the components while leaving the physical vector unchanged.
For ideal projectile motion without drag, horizontal velocity remains constant.|T|Gravity acts vertically, so there is no horizontal acceleration.
At a projectile’s highest point, its horizontal velocity must be zero.|F|Only the vertical velocity is zero there; horizontal motion can continue.
Horizontal and vertical projectile motions share the same elapsed time.|T|They are components of the same motion and must be evaluated at the same instant.
A projectile’s acceleration points along its velocity at every instant.|F|Acceleration points downward while velocity changes direction along the path.
Uniform circular motion has constant speed but changing velocity.|T|The velocity direction turns continuously.
Centripetal acceleration points toward the center of the circular path.|T|Its inward direction continuously changes the direction of velocity.
Doubling speed at fixed circular radius doubles centripetal acceleration.|F|Centripetal acceleration is proportional to speed squared, so it becomes four times larger.
Relative velocity depends on which observer is used.|T|In classical mechanics, changing the observer subtracts the observer’s velocity vector.
A particle’s position vector must point in the same direction as its velocity.|F|Position describes location from an origin, while velocity describes the current direction of motion.
Zero net force implies zero acceleration in an inertial frame.|T|Newton’s second law relates the vector sum of forces to mass times acceleration.
An object moving at constant velocity requires a forward net force.|F|Constant velocity requires zero net force; balanced forces can act while it moves.
Weight and mass are the same physical quantity.|F|Mass measures inertia; weight is the gravitational force on that mass.
The normal force is always equal to an object’s weight.|F|Its value depends on the other forces and acceleration perpendicular to the contact surface.
An action-reaction force pair acts on two different objects.|T|The forces are equal and opposite but do not cancel in a single-object force diagram.
An ideal massless rope over an ideal frictionless pulley has uniform tension.|T|These idealizations exclude mass and friction that could produce differing tensions.
A free-body diagram includes only forces acting on the selected object.|T|Forces the object exerts on other bodies belong in those other bodies’ diagrams.
Doubling net force at fixed mass doubles acceleration.|T|Acceleration is directly proportional to net force for constant mass.
Newton’s first law holds in every accelerating reference frame without additional terms.|F|It applies directly in inertial frames; accelerating frames require appropriate inertial-force terms.
Static friction always equals its maximum possible value.|F|It adjusts to the required value up to its maximum before slipping begins.
Kinetic friction opposes the relative sliding motion at a contact.|T|Its direction is determined by sliding of the surfaces relative to each other.
Centripetal force is an extra force added to gravity, tension, and friction.|F|It is the name for the inward resultant of the actual forces.
A car on a flat turn can receive its centripetal force from static friction.|T|Without sliding, tire-road friction can point inward and turn the car.
At terminal speed in vertical falling, acceleration is zero.|T|Drag and any buoyant force balance the downward weight.
Increasing the normal force can increase the kinetic-friction magnitude in the simple friction model.|T|That model gives kinetic friction as its coefficient times normal force.
The maximum static-friction coefficient has units of newtons.|F|A friction coefficient is a ratio of forces and is dimensionless.
A banked curve can reduce the friction needed to make a turn.|T|The tilted normal force can provide part or all of the required inward component.
An object traveling in a circle at constant speed has zero net force.|F|Its velocity changes direction, so a nonzero inward net force is required.
Kinetic energy is a scalar.|T|It depends on mass and speed squared, not the direction of velocity.
Doubling speed at fixed mass doubles kinetic energy.|F|Kinetic energy scales with speed squared, so it increases by a factor of four.
A force perpendicular to displacement does no work during that displacement.|T|The force-displacement dot product is zero.
Net negative work decreases kinetic energy.|T|The work-energy theorem equates net work to the change in kinetic energy.
A joule is equivalent to a newton-meter.|T|Work is force times displacement in the direction of the force.
Power is the rate at which work is done.|T|Its SI unit is the watt, equal to a joule per second.
A spring always does positive work.|F|It does negative work when motion stretches it farther from equilibrium and positive work when it releases stored energy.
Work by a variable force can be found from area under a force-position graph.|T|The signed area represents the integral of the force component over displacement.
Zero net work guarantees no forces acted.|F|Forces can do opposing work or act perpendicular to motion, leaving zero net work.
Gravitational potential energy depends on a chosen reference level.|T|Only potential-energy differences affect the work and motion predictions.
A conservative force’s work depends only on the endpoints.|T|Different connecting paths give the same work within the force’s domain.
Friction ordinarily converts mechanical energy into thermal energy.|T|Mechanical energy can decrease while the total energy of a complete isolated system remains conserved.
Potential energy is the same as force.|F|Force is related to how potential energy changes with position, not its value alone.
Near Earth, raising a mass by height h increases gravitational potential energy by mgh.|T|This approximation assumes a nearly constant gravitational field over the height change.
An ideal spring’s stored energy is proportional to its displacement from equilibrium.|F|It is proportional to displacement squared, with a factor of one-half times spring stiffness.
Stable equilibrium can occur at a local minimum of potential energy.|T|A small displacement then produces a restoring tendency toward the minimum.
Mechanical energy is always conserved even when external work is done.|F|External work or nonconservative processes can change a system’s mechanical energy.
At a turning point in one-dimensional conservative motion, kinetic energy is zero.|T|The particle momentarily stops along that coordinate before reversing direction.
The center of mass can lie outside the material of an object.|T|A ring’s center of mass lies in its empty central region.
Internal forces alone change the total momentum of an isolated system.|F|Internal action-reaction forces cancel; net external impulse changes total momentum.
Momentum is a vector.|T|Its direction is the velocity direction for positive mass.
Impulse equals the change in momentum.|T|Integrating net force over time gives the momentum change.
Total kinetic energy is conserved in every collision.|F|It is conserved in elastic collisions, but not generally in inelastic collisions.
Objects stick together in a perfectly inelastic collision.|T|They share a final velocity, while some kinetic energy becomes other forms of energy.
An explosion can increase total kinetic energy without changing total momentum of an isolated system.|T|Stored internal energy can become motion while the external impulse remains zero.
A longer stopping time reduces average force for the same momentum change.|T|Average force is impulse divided by the duration.
The center of mass accelerates according to the total external force.|T|Its acceleration equals that force divided by total mass.
All points of a rigid rotating body have the same angular velocity.|T|Rigid rotation preserves their relative angular positions.
All points of a rotating disk have the same linear speed.|F|Tangential speed increases with distance from the rotation axis.
Rotational inertia depends on how mass is distributed relative to the axis.|T|Mass farther from the axis contributes more through its squared distance.
Torque can be zero even when force is nonzero.|T|A force whose line of action passes through the axis has zero moment about it.
Doubling angular speed at fixed rotational inertia doubles rotational kinetic energy.|F|Rotational kinetic energy scales with angular speed squared and therefore quadruples.
Angular acceleration measures the rate of change of angular velocity.|T|Its SI unit is radians per second squared.
The parallel-axis theorem uses an axis through the center of mass as its reference.|T|The inertia about a parallel displaced axis equals central inertia plus mass times separation squared.
A radian is a length unit.|F|It is a dimensionless ratio of arc length to radius used to measure angles.
Net torque about a fixed axis equals rotational inertia times angular acceleration for a rigid body.|T|This is the rotational analogue of Newton’s second law for a fixed inertia.
A wheel rolling without slipping on a stationary floor satisfies center speed equals radius times angular speed.|T|The translational and rotational motions must match at the contact.

The contact point of a rolling wheel has zero acceleration because its instantaneous velocity is zero.|F|Zero instantaneous velocity does not imply zero acceleration; that point changes direction and motion.
A rolling object can have both translational and rotational kinetic energy.|T|Its center moves while the body also rotates about that center.
Angular momentum is conserved when net external torque is zero.|T|External torque determines the rate of change of angular momentum.
Pulling in the arms of an isolated spinning skater increases rotational inertia.|F|Moving mass toward the axis decreases inertia; angular speed rises to conserve angular momentum.
The angular momentum of a particle depends on the chosen origin.|T|It uses the position vector from that origin crossed with momentum.
The torque of a force can change when the reference point changes.|T|The lever arm is measured from the selected reference point.
A rigid body’s angular momentum is always parallel to its angular velocity.|F|They need not align for general rotation; alignment holds along principal axes.

Static friction must dissipate energy in ideal rolling without slipping on a stationary surface.|F|The contact point has no instantaneous motion relative to that surface, so ideal static friction there does no work.
Static equilibrium requires zero net force and zero net torque.|T|Both translational and rotational acceleration must vanish.
Zero net torque alone guarantees that an object is at rest.|F|It may translate, or rotate at constant angular velocity, depending on its state and other forces.
The same equilibrium calculation can use any torque origin.|T|When force balance also holds, a suitable origin can simplify the moment equation without changing the result.
Stress has units of force per area.|T|Its SI unit is the pascal, equivalent to newtons per square meter.
Strain is a dimensionless relative deformation.|T|It compares deformation with the original length or other appropriate reference measure.
Young’s modulus relates axial stress to axial strain in the linear elastic range.|T|Its value describes stiffness under tension or compression in that regime.
An elastic material always obeys Hooke’s law at every deformation.|F|Linear proportionality holds only within a limited range; large deformations can be nonlinear or permanent.
A couple consists of equal opposite forces with separated lines of action.|T|Its net force is zero but it can exert a nonzero torque.
A stable equilibrium tends to restore an object after a small disturbance.|T|A small displacement creates forces or torques directed back toward the equilibrium configuration.
Newton’s gravitational force between point masses falls with the square of separation.|T|Doubling separation reduces the force to one-quarter.
The gravitational field of Earth is exactly uniform at every altitude.|F|Its magnitude decreases with distance from Earth’s center outside the planet.
A satellite in circular orbit is continually accelerating.|T|Its velocity direction changes under inward gravitational acceleration.
Orbiting astronauts are weightless because Earth’s gravity is zero there.|F|They and their spacecraft are in shared free fall; gravity remains substantial in low orbit.
Escape speed from a spherical body depends on the escaping object’s mass.|F|Ignoring atmosphere and propulsion afterward, the object’s mass cancels from the energy equation.
Gravitational potential energy with zero at infinity is negative for two attracting finite-separated masses.|T|Energy must be supplied to separate them to infinity.
Kepler’s equal-area law means a planet moves faster when closer to the Sun.|T|Angular momentum conservation requires faster orbital motion at smaller distance.
For circular orbits around the same central mass, larger orbital radius means longer period.|T|Kepler’s third law gives period squared proportional to orbital radius cubed.
Inside an ideal uniform spherical shell, the shell’s gravitational field is zero.|T|The gravitational pulls from all parts of the shell cancel at every interior point.
Pressure in a fluid at rest acts normally on a submerged surface.|T|A static fluid cannot sustain a shear stress in equilibrium.
At equal depth in the same connected stationary liquid, pressure is equal.|T|For a uniform fluid under gravity, pressure depends on depth rather than container shape.
Gauge pressure includes atmospheric pressure by definition.|F|Gauge pressure is measured relative to atmospheric pressure; absolute pressure includes it.
Buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid.|T|The net pressure force is given by Archimedes’ principle.
A floating object displaces a fluid weight equal to its own weight.|T|In static floating equilibrium, buoyancy balances weight.
An incompressible steady flow speeds up when the flow area narrows.|T|Continuity requires volume flow rate to remain constant along the stream tube.
Bernoulli’s simple equation applies to every viscous turbulent flow without correction.|F|It assumes idealized conditions such as negligible viscous losses along a streamline.
An object’s buoyant force must equal its own weight even while it is sinking with acceleration.|F|Equality is an equilibrium condition; a sinking accelerating object can have unequal forces.
Pressure is measured in pascals.|T|One pascal equals one newton per square meter.
Simple harmonic acceleration points toward equilibrium.|T|It is proportional to displacement with the opposite sign.
At the equilibrium position of an ideal spring oscillator, speed is greatest.|T|Potential energy is minimal there, leaving maximum kinetic energy.
At maximum displacement, a harmonic oscillator has maximum speed.|F|The oscillator is at a turning point, so its instantaneous speed is zero.
An ideal linear spring’s oscillation period is independent of amplitude.|T|Within the linear model, period depends on mass and stiffness rather than amplitude.
Doubling an ideal spring oscillator’s mass increases its period.|T|The period scales with the square root of mass.
A simple pendulum’s usual amplitude-independent period formula assumes small angles.|T|At larger angles the small-angle approximation fails and the period changes.
Damping makes mechanical energy of an unforced oscillator decrease.|T|Resistive effects convert mechanical energy into other forms.
Driving near a system’s natural frequency can produce a large response.|T|Resonance occurs when repeated forcing transfers energy effectively, with damping limiting the response.
Frequency and period are equal quantities.|F|Frequency is the reciprocal of period: cycles per second versus seconds per cycle.
A transverse wave has oscillations perpendicular to its propagation direction.|T|A wave on a taut string is a common example.
Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength.|T|Each period the pattern advances one wavelength.
Increasing frequency always increases the wave speed on the same ideal taut string.|F|String wave speed is set by tension and mass per unit length in the ideal model.
A pulse carries a permanent chunk of string along with it.|F|The disturbance travels while string elements oscillate near their own equilibrium positions.
Superposition adds overlapping wave displacements in a linear medium.|T|Interference follows from adding their instantaneous signed displacements.
Two equal waves exactly out of phase can cancel their displacement.|T|A crest of one coincides with an equal trough of the other.
A standing wave has locations that remain at zero displacement.|T|These nodes result from sustained destructive interference.
A string fixed at both ends has displacement antinodes at those endpoints.|F|Fixed endpoints cannot move, so they are nodes.
Increasing string tension at fixed linear density increases wave speed.|T|The speed is proportional to the square root of tension.
Sound in an ordinary fluid is a longitudinal pressure wave.|T|Particle oscillations are along the propagation direction.
Sound can propagate through a perfect vacuum.|F|Sound requires a material medium to carry pressure disturbances.
Sound intensity is power per area.|T|Its SI unit is watts per square meter.
Doubling distance from an ideal point source in open space reduces intensity to one-quarter.|T|The same power spreads over a spherical area proportional to distance squared.
A 10-decibel increase represents ten times the sound intensity.|T|The intensity-level scale uses ten times the base-ten logarithm of the intensity ratio.
The Doppler effect can change the observed frequency without changing the source’s emitted frequency.|T|Relative motion changes how quickly wavefronts reach the observer.
Beats arise from adding waves of nearly equal frequencies.|T|Their changing relative phase produces alternating louder and quieter sound.
A closed end of an ideal air column is a displacement node.|T|Air cannot oscillate through the solid boundary, although pressure variation can be large there.
Pitch and loudness describe exactly the same wave property.|F|Pitch relates mainly to frequency; loudness relates to intensity and hearing response.
Thermal equilibrium means two contacting bodies have no net heat transfer between them.|T|They have equal temperature, so there is no temperature-driven net exchange.
Heat is a substance stored inside an object.|F|Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; internal energy is a state property.
A temperature difference of one kelvin equals a difference of one Celsius degree.|T|Their increments have the same size even though their zero points differ.
The Celsius temperature can be inserted directly into every ideal-gas formula.|F|Thermodynamic temperature must be expressed on an absolute scale, normally kelvin.
A phase change can absorb heat without changing temperature.|T|At the transition conditions, energy changes the phase rather than raising temperature.
Specific heat describes energy needed per mass per temperature change.|T|For constant specific heat without a phase change, heat equals mass times specific heat times temperature change.
Thermal conduction requires bulk transport of the material.|F|Conduction transfers energy through microscopic interactions; convection involves bulk movement.
Radiation can transfer thermal energy across a vacuum.|T|Electromagnetic radiation does not require a material medium.
Thermal expansion always causes a hole in a uniformly heated metal plate to shrink.|F|Under free uniform expansion, the hole expands as if filled with the same expanding material.
Ideal-gas pressure results from molecular momentum transfer to the container walls.|T|Collisions exert forces whose time average produces pressure.
At equal temperature, all gas molecules have exactly the same speed.|F|Molecular speeds follow a distribution even at thermal equilibrium.
Average translational kinetic energy of an ideal-gas molecule depends on absolute temperature.|T|It equals three-halves Boltzmann’s constant times temperature for three translational dimensions.
At equal temperature, lighter gas molecules generally have greater root-mean-square speed.|T|The mean translational energy is the same, so smaller mass corresponds to larger squared speed.
An ideal gas’s internal energy depends only on temperature.|T|The idealization neglects intermolecular potential-energy dependence on volume.
An isothermal expansion of an ideal gas has zero change in internal energy.|T|Temperature is unchanged, so the ideal gas’s internal energy remains unchanged.
Adiabatic means constant temperature.|F|Adiabatic means no heat transfer; temperature can still change through work.
Mean free path describes an average distance between molecular collisions.|T|It is a statistical measure, not the identical distance traveled by every molecule.
The ideal-gas approximation is usually best at high density near condensation.|F|It is generally better at low density where molecular volume and interactions are less important.
Entropy is a state function.|T|Its change depends on the end states, not the path taken between them.
The entropy of an isolated system cannot decrease in a spontaneous macroscopic process.|T|It increases for irreversible processes and remains constant for ideal reversible processes.
A system’s entropy can decrease if its surroundings gain enough entropy.|T|The second-law restriction applies to the combined isolated total, not every part separately.
A heat engine can convert all absorbed heat into work in a cyclic single-reservoir process.|F|The Kelvin–Planck statement of the second law rules this out.
A refrigerator moves heat from colder to warmer regions by requiring work.|T|The work input allows the transfer while satisfying the second law.
Carnot efficiency depends on the reservoir temperatures in kelvin.|T|Absolute temperatures set the maximum possible efficiency between those reservoirs.
Every reversible engine between the same two reservoirs has the same efficiency.|T|Otherwise combining two such engines could violate the second law.
Free expansion of an ideal gas into a vacuum is reversible.|F|It is irreversible, even though internal energy may remain unchanged in an insulated setup.
Entropy can increase when two different gases mix.|T|Mixing increases the number of accessible microscopic arrangements under the usual ideal-gas conditions.
Like electric charges repel and unlike charges attract.|T|The sign of the product of two charges determines the direction of the Coulomb interaction.
Electric charge is conserved in an isolated system.|T|Charge can move between objects but the isolated total remains unchanged.
A neutral object contains no charged particles.|F|Its positive and negative charges balance overall.
Coulomb’s force between point charges in vacuum varies inversely with separation squared.|T|Doubling the separation reduces the force magnitude by a factor of four.
Doubling one point charge doubles the electric-force magnitude when everything else is fixed.|T|Coulomb’s law is proportional to the product of the charges.
A conductor allows some charges to move relatively freely.|T|Mobile charge carriers can redistribute through the material.
An insulator can never become electrically charged.|F|Charge can be deposited on an insulator even though it does not move freely through it.
Charging by friction creates net charge from nothing.|F|It transfers charge between materials while preserving the total.
The elementary-charge magnitude is positive even though an electron’s charge is negative.|T|The electron has charge −e, where e denotes the positive elementary magnitude.
The electric field direction is the force direction on a positive test charge.|T|A negative test charge experiences force opposite to that field direction.
Doubling a test charge doubles the electric field produced by the source charges.|F|The source field is independent of a sufficiently small test charge; the test force doubles instead.
Electric fields from multiple sources add as vectors.|T|Superposition requires adding components, not just field magnitudes.
The electric field of a positive point charge points outward.|T|A positive test charge is repelled from the source.
A point where electric potential is zero must also have zero electric field.|F|Potential value depends on reference; field depends on spatial changes in potential.
An electric dipole has equal and opposite separated charges.|T|Its net charge is zero but its spatial charge separation creates a field.
A uniform electric field can exert a torque on an electric dipole.|T|Opposite forces on separated charges can rotate it even with zero net force.
Electric field lines intersect wherever the field is strongest.|F|An intersection would assign two field directions to one point; field lines do not cross.
The SI unit of electric field can be written as newtons per coulomb.|T|Field is electric force divided by test charge.
Gauss’s law relates total electric flux through a closed surface to enclosed net charge.|T|The closed-surface flux equals enclosed charge divided by vacuum permittivity.
Charges outside a closed surface can affect the electric field on that surface.|T|Their net flux through the whole surface is zero, but their local field need not vanish.
Zero net electric flux guarantees zero electric field everywhere on the surface.|F|Field can enter and leave in equal amounts, giving zero total flux without vanishing locally.
The area vector for a closed Gaussian surface is conventionally outward.|T|Outward field contributions then count positively in the flux integral.
Gauss’s law is valid only for spherical charge distributions.|F|It is general; symmetry determines whether it provides an easy way to calculate the field.
Inside the material of an electrostatic conductor, the electric field is zero.|T|A nonzero internal field would keep free charges moving, contradicting electrostatic equilibrium.
Excess charge on an isolated electrostatic conductor resides on its surfaces.|T|Free charges redistribute until the field vanishes within the conducting material.
Electric flux is the same physical quantity as electric field.|F|Flux measures field through an oriented area and has different units from field.
A larger Gaussian surface enclosing the same charge has the same net flux.|T|The enclosed charge fixes total flux even if the field strength varies across different surfaces.
Electric potential is potential energy per unit charge.|T|A volt equals a joule per coulomb.
Electric potential is a vector.|F|It is a scalar; potentials add algebraically rather than as vectors.
Electric field points toward decreasing potential locally.|T|The field is the negative spatial gradient of potential.
Moving along an equipotential requires no work by the electrostatic force.|T|The potential difference and corresponding electric potential-energy change are zero.
An equipotential surface is perpendicular to the electric field wherever the field is nonzero.|T|The field has no tangential component along a constant-potential surface.
A negative charge always accelerates in the direction of decreasing potential under electric force alone.|F|Its force opposes the field, so its initial acceleration is toward increasing potential.
Choosing a different zero for potential changes the electric field.|F|Adding a constant to potential leaves spatial differences and the field unchanged.
A positive point charge has positive potential when zero is chosen at infinity.|T|Its potential is proportional to positive charge divided by distance.
Zero work around a closed path is consistent with an electrostatic conservative field.|T|The starting and ending potentials are identical, so the net potential-energy change is zero.
Capacitance is charge magnitude divided by potential difference.|T|It describes stored charge per volt for a specified capacitor geometry and dielectric.
The SI unit of capacitance is the farad.|T|One farad equals one coulomb per volt.
Increasing plate area increases ideal parallel-plate capacitance at fixed separation.|T|Capacitance is proportional to plate area in that model.
Increasing plate separation increases ideal parallel-plate capacitance.|F|Capacitance is inversely proportional to separation when area and dielectric are fixed.
Capacitors in parallel have capacitances that add.|T|They share a voltage, and their stored charges add.
Identical capacitors in series have a total capacitance larger than either one.|F|Their series capacitance is smaller; two identical ones give half the individual capacitance.
Energy stored in a capacitor is proportional to voltage squared at fixed capacitance.|T|Stored energy is one-half capacitance times voltage squared.
Inserting a dielectric into a disconnected charged capacitor increases its voltage.|F|With charge fixed, the increased capacitance lowers the voltage.
An ideal dielectric polarizes in an applied electric field.|T|Bound positive and negative charges shift slightly relative to each other, altering the field response.
Conventional current points in the direction positive charge would move.|T|In a metal, electron drift is in the opposite direction.
One ampere equals one coulomb per second.|T|Current is the rate of charge passing a cross section.
Current density is current per cross-sectional area for uniform perpendicular flow.|T|The more general current is the surface integral of current density dotted with area.
A metal wire’s electrons must move near light speed for a circuit to respond quickly.|F|Drift is slow; the electromagnetic signal establishing the field propagates much faster.
Ohm’s law describes a linear voltage-current relation for an ohmic component at fixed conditions.|T|Temperature and material state must remain suitable for constant resistance.
Doubling a uniform wire’s length at fixed area and resistivity doubles its resistance.|T|Resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to area.
Resistance and resistivity are identical quantities with identical units.|F|Resistivity is a material property; resistance also depends on geometry.
A resistor dissipates power equal to current times voltage across it.|T|Equivalent expressions use current squared times resistance or voltage squared divided by resistance.
All materials have resistance that increases with temperature in the same way.|F|Temperature dependence differs among metals, semiconductors, and other materials.
At a steady-state circuit junction, total incoming current equals total outgoing current.|T|Charge conservation prevents a persistent buildup at the junction.
The sum of signed potential changes around a simple steady DC loop is zero.|T|Kirchhoff’s loop rule expresses energy conservation in the lumped circuit model.
Resistors in series carry the same current.|T|A single uninterrupted path gives no junction where current can split.
Resistors in parallel share the same potential difference.|T|Both ends of each branch connect to the same two nodes.
Current is used up as it passes through a resistor.|F|Charge flow is conserved; electrical energy is transferred in the resistor.
Adding a parallel resistor increases equivalent resistance.|F|An additional conducting path reduces the equivalent resistance.
An ideal capacitor carries a sustained nonzero current after reaching a constant-voltage DC steady state.|F|Once its charge stops changing, capacitor current is zero in the ideal model.
An RC time constant equals resistance times capacitance.|T|It sets the characteristic time scale for exponential charging or discharging.
An ideal battery has zero internal resistance.|T|Its terminal voltage equals its specified emf regardless of current in the idealization.
The magnetic force on a moving point charge is perpendicular to its velocity.|T|The cross product of velocity and magnetic field gives that direction.
A stationary charge experiences a magnetic force from a static magnetic field alone.|F|The magnetic part of the Lorentz force vanishes when velocity is zero.
A magnetic force alone can change a particle’s kinetic energy.|F|It is perpendicular to velocity and does no work, although it can change the direction of motion.
A charge moving parallel to a magnetic field experiences zero magnetic force.|T|The cross product is zero for parallel or antiparallel vectors.
Reversing the charge sign reverses the magnetic-force direction at fixed velocity and field.|T|The force is directly proportional to signed charge.
A current-carrying wire can experience a force in a magnetic field.|T|Magnetic forces on its moving charge carriers transfer to the wire.
A magnetic dipole can experience torque in a uniform magnetic field.|T|The torque tends to align its magnetic moment with the field.
The radius of circular motion in a uniform field grows with particle momentum at fixed charge and field.|T|The radius equals perpendicular momentum divided by charge magnitude times field magnitude.
The magnetic field unit is the tesla.|T|Its units are consistent with force divided by charge times speed.
A long straight current-carrying wire produces magnetic field lines that circle the wire.|T|The right-hand rule relates the circulation direction to conventional current.
Doubling current doubles magnetic field in the ideal long-wire model.|T|Field magnitude is directly proportional to current.
The long-wire magnetic field falls with distance squared.|F|For an ideal infinitely long wire, field magnitude is inversely proportional to perpendicular distance.
Two long parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction attract.|T|Each wire’s magnetic field exerts an inward force on the other current.
Opposite parallel currents attract in the same manner as matching currents.|F|They repel rather than attract.
An ideal long solenoid has an approximately uniform internal magnetic field away from its ends.|T|The contributions of many closely spaced turns combine into a nearly uniform axial field.
Ampère’s simple magnetostatic law is easiest to use when symmetry constrains the field.|T|Useful symmetry can make the field constant and tangent along parts of the chosen loop.
Magnetic fields from multiple currents add as vectors.|T|Superposition combines the direction and magnitude of every source contribution.
The Biot–Savart law assigns field contributions to current elements.|T|Integrating those contributions gives the magnetic field of the specified steady current distribution.
A changing magnetic flux through a loop can induce an emf.|T|Faraday’s law relates induced emf to the rate of flux change.
Lenz’s law makes induced current reinforce the change that produced it.|F|Its direction opposes the change in flux, consistent with energy conservation.
Magnetic flux can change because a loop changes orientation in a fixed field.|T|Flux depends on field direction relative to the loop’s area vector.
A loop must be stationary for Faraday’s law to apply.|F|Flux changes can result from motion, deformation, or a changing magnetic field.
An inductor resists changes in current.|T|Its self-induced emf opposes the current’s rate of change rather than the current itself.
Energy stored in an ideal inductor is proportional to current squared.|T|It equals one-half inductance times current squared.
The RL time constant is inductance divided by resistance.|T|That ratio determines the rate of current’s exponential approach to steady state.
An induced electric field from changing magnetic flux must be conservative.|F|It can have a nonzero closed-loop circulation and cannot generally be described by a single scalar potential alone.
